lesson_title: Radius, Diameter, Circumference, Area and the Meaning of Pi
hook_text: A coin, a plate, a bucket. Five objects, one hidden number — she found it with a strip of paper.
clip_script:
For a Grade 8 investigation, a learner in Mahikeng is asked to find pi from measurements of round objects at home. She wraps a paper strip around a plate, a tin, a bucket, a coin and a mug, and divides each circumference by its diameter.

Plate: 3,14. Bucket: 3,15. Tin, mug, coin: all between 3,13 and 3,16. A coin and a bucket, wildly different sizes, and the same ratio every time. That ratio is pi — the number of diameters that fit around any circle. Its decimals never end, so 3,14 is only ever an approximation.
visual_style: Kitchen objects on a table; a paper strip unwraps from each into a straight line beside its diameter, and the ratios stack up near 3,14
call_to_action: Open the full session to see where every circle formula comes from.
